title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
author: Frederick Douglass
openingText: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot County, Maryland. I have no reliable knowledge of my own age, since I have never seen any official record of it. Most slaves know as little about their ages as horses do about theirs, and nearly every master I knew of wanted to keep them that ignorant. I cannot remember ever meeting a slave who could name his birthday. The closest they ever come is something like planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring, or fall. Not knowing my own age troubled me even as a child. The white children could state theirs, and I could not see why I should be denied the same privilege. I was not allowed to ask my master about it. He considered any such question from a slave improper, impertinent, and a sign of a restless spirit. My nearest estimate puts me now at between twenty-seven and twenty-eight, which I reach because I once heard my master say, sometime in 1835, that I was about seventeen.
about:
Published in 1845, Frederick Douglass’s account follows his life in slavery in Maryland, his escape in 1838, and the beginnings of his public work against slavery. He names people and places, describes violence he witnessed and endured, and explains how the system denied enslaved people knowledge, family ties, and the fruits of their work.

In Baltimore, Sophia Auld begins teaching him to read until her husband forbids it. Douglass continues learning in secret. Later, resistance to Edward Covey becomes a turning point in his sense of himself. Friendship, collective plans, paid work, and the help of others also matter to his pursuit of freedom. He deliberately withholds the details of his successful escape to protect people and routes still in use.

The closing appendix distinguishes the Christianity Douglass values from the religion used to defend slavery. Its poems and biblical quotations extend the argument of the narrative. This edition contains his eleven chapters and appendix; the original volume’s prefatory contributions by William Lloyd Garrison and Wendell Phillips are not included in the reader text.

angleCards.title: Learning to read
angleCards.text: Hugh Auld warns that reading will make Douglass unfit to be a slave. Douglass takes the warning as a guide. I want to follow how literacy creates possibilities while making captivity more painful.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Douglass’s efforts to read and write and examine how knowledge changes his understanding of slavery.

angleCards.title: Power and the slaveholder
angleCards.text: Sophia Auld initially treats Douglass kindly, but later opposes his reading. I want to examine his explanation of her change and compare her with the other slaveholders.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Douglass’s argument that slavery also corrupts those who hold power within it.

angleCards.title: Resistance and fellowship
angleCards.text: The fight with Covey is a turning point, but Douglass also describes friendships, teaching, and shared escape plans. I want to consider both individual action and mutual help.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Covey episode alongside Douglass’s relationships with other enslaved people to consider different forms of resistance.

angleCards.title: Faith and hypocrisy
angleCards.text: The appendix clarifies that Douglass attacks religion used to defend slavery. I want to read its biblical quotations and satire alongside his accounts of religious slaveholders.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Douglass distinguishes Christ’s Christianity from slaveholding religion and uses faith in his criticism.

cast.name: Frederick Douglass
cast.description: Douglass recalls his life in slavery and his efforts to gain freedom. He distinguishes what he witnessed from what he heard or inferred, and withholds escape details that might endanger others.

cast.name: Sophia Auld
cast.role: The woman who begins teaching him
cast.description: Hugh Auld’s wife in Baltimore. She initially teaches Douglass his letters, but follows her husband’s prohibition and later actively prevents him from reading. He also describes her renewed kindness after he is assaulted.

cast.name: Hugh Auld
cast.description: He forbids Douglass’s reading lessons and takes his shipyard wages. After white apprentices attack Douglass, he seeks redress, only to encounter the refusal to accept Black testimony against white men.

cast.name: Edward Covey
cast.role: The farmer known for breaking slaves
cast.description: A farmer who rents enslaved workers and has a reputation for breaking their resistance. Douglass describes relentless work, violence, and surveillance, followed by the fight after which Covey stops whipping him.

cast.name: Thomas Auld
cast.description: He acquires enslaved people through marriage and sends Douglass to Covey. Douglass describes his religious conversion as intensifying his cruelty and giving him a justification for it.

cast.name: Anna Murray
cast.description: A free woman who joins him in New York after his escape. They marry there and travel together to New Bedford to begin their life in freedom.

acclaim.quote: This Narrative contains many affecting incidents, many passages of great eloquence and power.
acclaim.context: Preface to the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

whyItMatters.title: Testimony with limits made explicit
whyItMatters.body: Douglass offers names, places, remembered dialogue, and uncertainty where he lacks knowledge. His refusal to explain his escape shows that telling the truth also involves responsibilities toward people still at risk.

whyItMatters.title: Learning, labour, and freedom
whyItMatters.body: Reading helps Douglass understand his condition, but does not immediately release him from it. The account also follows work, wages taken by an owner, collective resistance, and the precarious position of a fugitive in the North.

whyItMatters.title: An argument within Christianity
whyItMatters.body: The appendix rejects the use of faith to excuse slavery while affirming Douglass’s own Christianity. Biblical quotation and satire sharpen the contrast between professed belief and conduct.
